Difficult to tell extent of Roman workings, given that there was prehistoric mining as well. The local mining villages had imported shells and bowls from the 2nd and 3rd centuries. New infrastructure was created for the mines including roads, settlements and forts. Specialist contractors brought in after military establishment. The oppidum was involved in mine workings but whether this was under imperial control is unknown

Large hydraulic system employed with multiple leats. Probably this mine did not continue operations into the imperial period. Roads were built connecting the settlements and mines as well as providing extra regional travel. Nearby are located stone structures which could be workers' hamlets (over 250 groups). Pliny notes a Rebublican law forbidding the use of more than 5000 workers in a single mine, which might indicate that prior to this rule more had been present.

Known as Phaeno in Roman times. A copper mining site located in the Wadi Faynan off the Wadi ‘Arabah. Peak production was in the fourth century which is later than most mining sites especially those in the western empire. The underground mining was extensive and the mine of Umm al-Amad is one of the largest known mine galleries in the Roman empire. An estimated 2,500-7,000 tons of copper were produced here.
Open trenches and underground galleries, with stepped descent. Some shafts up to 70 m deep. Large exploitation chamber.

Work started shortly after conquest in the 1st century BC then lasted until the 3rd century AD. Corta de Covas opencast, 430 m in length, 2.3 million m³ removed. Traces of firesetting at the base. Underground galleries for ore extraction, and prospection. Peak extraction dates to first half of second century AD. Anvil stones from Roman water-powered ore-crushing machines have been found.

Nearby is located a Roman mining settlement (under Baia de Cris). At Caraci iron tools, possibly Roman, were found. Some evidence for water leats was recorded but it is not clear to what this refers.
Originally found were Roman buildings which are no longer existing. Tools and miners' lamps were also found.

Extensive subterranean silver mine. Roman structures including hydraulic tanks and buildings were recorded in the 19th century but they are no longer visible. Galleries were approximately 2 m high and 0.56–0.65 m wide. Finds discovered include mining tools, lamps, mosaics, tiles and mural paintings in the nearby buildings.
Roman gallery on the slope of the Ghergheleului with a ceiling width of 42 cm, a width of 75 cm in the middle, a width of 85 cm, a height of 1.95 cm (the floor is not reached), and worked in steps.
Mining settlement (exploitation) of Băiţa-Măgura. Mining, extraction and administrative center (about 20 buildings, canals and a rainwater collection basin).

"Roman buildings and artefacts related to the exploitation of the stone were reported here. According to some information, gold sands have been washed here to select the precious metal." - Luca 2008, 32 (translated).
Roman mine gallery.  Intrarea în galerie este prăbuşită.
Roman mine gallery. This gallery links with the exploitation of Magdana Hill in the village of Trestia. The mouth of the gallery is collapsing.
It was reported in the late 1800s that Roman structures existed and evidence for mining included tools. Gold washing was said to have taken place.
Mostly a site of iron mining, but gold, silver, and tin were also exploited. Found nearby were miners' lamps and bricks stamped by the Legio IV Flavia Felix.
Quartz-vein opencast, 600 m long and up to 40 m deep. Channels and hushing tanks on the eastern edge (said by Ciugudean to be for ore-processing; but this happens downhill, in the Poduri area).
Channels and ponds for ore processing visible on Google Earth. Probable slag heap to SW.
Roman mine gallery (galeria Petru şi Pavel / Peter and Paul gallery) with trapezoidal cross-section. In 1929 or 1930 the hub and some spokes of a wooden water-lifting wheel were found.
Roman and modern mine gallery.  The gallery runs E-W; it is flooded; width c. 1.5 m, length c. 60 m.
Roman and modern mine gallery, flooded, with a height of c. 1.20 m.
Mine workings existed on many of the surrounding hills. Coins and Roman bricks were found as well.
Roman workings. "In the “Valea Şteampurilor” spot one can see sand and gravel mounds resulted from" - sIMION 2006: 136.
Roman settlements surround the mine. Piles of debris from washing the gold ore are present on the surface near the mines. "Mining exploitation point - Marcul (surface mining)." - Simion 2006: 136
Roman mine galleries, and cemetery at Cinciş.
Surface exploitation. Steril de granulaţie mică .
Hydraulic mining, partly re-using ditch of castro (misinterpreted by Fanzul Perada as evidence for pre-Roman hydraulic mining)
Google Earth shows extensive stone dumps or murias.

"As in the case of San Finx, these mines were worked by the ancients,  the method being to open up a trench or cast on the back of the lode,  thus forming a pile on either side""; ""cavernous workings were sometimes resorted to"". (Borlase 1897: 17). (This is what Borlase refers to as the "Tyre and Sidon" reservation near Fontao and Merza.)"

Located in the Mazarron region it was a huge mining area as indicated by the archaeological remains of buildings, workings and mining waste (over 2.4 million tons). It had galleries measuring over 2 km in length. It was opened in the Republican period and was leased to mining companies.
Underground adit driven into hillside; prospection?

Large underground Roman silver and lead mine. Based on archeaological finds including coins the mining started in the 2nd century BC. Five Archimedes’ screws have been found along with mining tools. The mines went to a depth of 225 metres.
Castro immediately adjacent to mine, possible gully issuing from ditch at South.
Piriform opencast. Castro of El Saldonal nearby (42.446088, -6.144155).
Google Earth shows an area worked out by hushing or ground-sluicing; and a possible corona to the East.
Google Earth suggests that the mine is adjacent to/imbircated with a corona.
Numerous channels and stone dumps from ground sluicing, visible on Google Earth.
Remains of a mine and smelteries found
Large and deep opencast fed by multiple aqueducts, with hushing tanks.
Sizeable mining zone, largely destroyed by 19th/20th-c. works
Large alluvial ruina montium mine, with some reworking of the downhill parts in the late 19th century.
Extensive area of rake/comb workings along tributary of the Rio Duerna

Several hydraulic opencasts; two on the N side of the valley; a large one on the S side, and a smaller piriform opencast to the S of that. In the main, S, opencast there are subterranean galleries opening off the side of the opencast.
Aqueduct and hushing opencast visible on Google Earth.
Very large opencase worked by ruina montium technique; one tunnel still visible towards northern end of east face of opencast. Mine supplied by aqueduct said to be c. 40 km long.

3 main aqueducts fed this mine; one is 21.5 km long from Murias de Ponjos, and another 17.5 km from Ponjos. http://www.diariodeleon.es/noticias/cultura/identifican-mas-50-kilometros-canalizacion-romana-omana_535566.html
Extensive hydraulic mining in alluvial deposits. Castro immediately adjacent to mine.

Located in the Salamanca district, over 40km of hydraulic channels have been recorded. Dossier IV. Mostly exploitation was by hushing but also some open cast and underground mines were worked. Approximately 2.5 million cubic metres of material were moved.
Opencast pit nearly 20 m deep; volume of earth extracted calculated at 1083 m3 from LiDAR survey.
The river Sil was diverted to expose the placer deposits. Where the river made a sharp turn it was diverted through a rock-cut tunnel.
I have assumed that Navelgas Nord = the Mina de Entrepeñas, underground gallery; usually flooded.
Possible hydraulic opencast mining visible on Google Earth
Hydraulic mining - opencast and hushing tank, directly next to earlier castro.
Opencast pit from hard rock mining, now flooded.
Hushing tank and hush gulley, aqueduct channels for collecting snow melt.
Rake ground-sluicing, and hushing using ditches of pre-Roman castro
Overgrown; stone piles visible on Google Earth
Hushing, developed out of ditches of Los Castellones hillfort

Originally a Punic mine, Riotinto was one of the largest mines in the Roman empire. It may be the site that Ptolemy refers to as Urium. Silver and copper mine which produced an estimated 16,000,000 tons of slag. 16 pairs of water wheels found in the mine draining depths of 100m. It is surrounded by an extensive settlement with cemeteries.

Large ruina montium workings, with a front of c. 995 m supplied by an aqueduct 18.3 km long and 1.5 m wide, feeding at least 5 reservoirs. Several vertical shafts for ruina montium working have been traced along the summit behind the working face, and remains of a gallery in the opencast face confirm ruina montium technique.

A large Roman mine noted for its many shafts - 100 twin shafts and 50 single shafts. To drain the mines water-lifting devices were used; remains of an Archimedes screw and a pump have been found. Smelting activities produced an estimated 40,000 tons of slag.
Probably largely destroyed by modern mine.

Extraction started at Tharsis in the Iron Age, circa 2500 BC. The zenith of production was under Trajan but coins which have been found suggest mining could have continued until AD 350. The site has large slag piles and an estimated 4,000,000 tonnes of slag were produced. Other finds include remains of a water wheel with a rope still attached. After the Visigoths invaded the difficulty in draining the mine may have made it unworkable and been the cause of its closure.
Fed by aqueduct channel. Matias mentions 7 reservoir tanks, and an anvil stone with 4 stamp depressions.

Hydraulic mine apparently re-using ditches of the Castro de Pelou (Sanchez-Palencia quoted as saying that the castro owes its existence to the mines and that its ditches were excavated by hydraulic means; which must be wrong: ditches re-used as hushing reservoirs.
Cavers found a 4th-century coin hoard at Engine Vein.

A road leading to town and fort and workings has been identified. An imperial freedman's gravestone indicates imperial control of mines. Inscribed lead ingots have been excavated with the names of companies or of the transporters of the lead. The emperors Claudius, Nero, and Vespasian are named on lead ingots.

A Roman gold mine located in Pumsaint, Wales operating from the first through the third century. The nearby fort (2 ha) probably oversaw the mining operation and suggest imperial control of the mines. However civilian contractors probably worked the mines later. A large hydraulic system was set up with multiple tanks and 5 aqueducts, one over 11 km in length, for exploiting the opencast pits. Underground mining also took place to considerable depths and pieces of a water wheel used to drain the mines were found in the 1930’s. Bath house and workshops found near the mines. The Carreg Pumpsaint is an anvil stone from a Roman ore-crushing machine, located next to a heap of crushed ore slimes, and a wheel-race fed from a dammed pond.

Roads, settlements and forts created by specialist contractors brought in after military establishment. 33 denarii of Antonius Pius and coins of Constantine were found. Roads and track ways leading between Great Orme and the Chester (Deva) fort.
Gallery extending nearly 120 m underground. Roman counterfeit coinage produced here.

The creation of roads, settlements and forts suggests specialist contractors brought in after establishment by military. Towers and a fort, Caer Gybi, are located nearby as well as a Fort at Chester (Deva) to the east this indicates a high degree of military control. However there is evidence that civilians were involved in the mining.
Coins of Antoninus Pius found as well as Hadrianic ingots have been found.
(There is gold in the deposits, now exploited, but apparently not recovered by the Romans). 3 smelting furnaces found. 11 million tonnes of slag produced.

Traces of opencast mining and extensive smelting slag predating 18th-c. exploitation. Spread of smelting slag dated by radiocarbon dates of 60 BC to AD 90 and AD 20-220 (95.4%).  Roman ore crushing anvil, Carreg Angharad Fychan, nearby. Roman fort 200 m from mine.
Remains of ancient mine workings identified near Azinieres in 1961, dated to 1st c. AD by La Graufesenque terra sigillata.
Lead mining and smelting; nearby settlement at Pentre. Furnaces recorded in 1840s, Halkyn Mountain. Lead pigs with stamps of Deceangli.
Ground sluicing to expose quartz or quartite veins. Hadrianic lead ingots found in vicinity. Nearby fort at Brompton is late 1st century to Hadrianic.
Opencast mines ("scowles"") and tunnels; probably 3rd-c. AD. 4th-c. temple"
Reservoir fed by two parallel aqueducts. (Possibly these are visible on Google Earth to the SE, at e.g.  43.967648, 17.702180)
Late Roman tin ingot found nearby.

Vertical shaft c. 50 ft deep; Main Passage 300 ft long and between 18 in and 20 ft high, and chambers full of miners' deads. Five possible openings to the surface including the shaft through which the mine was discovered in 1965. Two late 3rd-c. coins and counterfeiting material found around a hearth that post-dates the abandonment of the mine.

Work started shortly after conquest in the 1st century BC then lasted until the 3rd century AD. Corta de Ribeirinha, large opencast 370 m in length, 2.5 million m³ removed,  Traces of firesetting at the base. Underground galleries for ore extraction, and prospection. Peak extraction dates to first half of second century AD. Anvil stones from Roman water-powered ore-crushing machines have been found.
A large underground exploitation chamber, whose roof has collapsed so that it now resembles an opencast. Further prospection galleries, shafts, and underground workings.
Trench mining along a vein, for c. 3.5 km; splits into several trenches towards the west.
Mining dumps and a large spread of slag from smelting, together with ore-crushing anvils, indicating an underground mine whose entrance remains obscured by vegetations.
Castro with double ditches, later worked by hydraulic means with additional channels, deepening of ditches, and opencast on eastern side.
Cinnabar mine, probably part of an imperial estate: tunnel collapsed in antiquity, killing nearly 50 people.
Old mining works, including c. 30 circular shafts which may be the West Devon black tin mine that must have been active in the Roman period._x000D_
Gold mine - Maidan at Brădişoru de Jos
Roman mine at Creaca - Cariera Creaca Ţiclar
Iron mine of the Daco-Roman period at Criciova.

Mining at Hărgănani- Magura Baii. Open gallery with shaft about 20-30 m down. On the northeast wall are visible traces of exploitation with chisel and hammer (possibly Roman). The shaft has wooden reinforcement and the ceiling is supported by wooden reinforcement.
Mining at Hărgănani- Magura Baii. Mine gallery.

Roman mining at Hărgănani- Magura Baii. 'At a distance of about 2 m from the entrance mouth, traces of exploitation with the chisel and hammer are visible. At about 5 m from the entrance mouth opens a gallery completely clogged with mining tailings and boulders (about 10-20 cm). It is not possible to say with precision whether it is a Roman gallery. The forward direction is NNE - SSV. At the mouth of the gallery is a mining tailings with a very fine yellowish gray grain.' (RAN)
Hărţăgani-Măgura Băii. Mine tailings visible on the surface, small grain size.

Roman-era mine at Mesteacăn, com. Răchitova.

At 'La Poduri' is 'a cave that functioned as a mine at an unknown period.'
Roman iron mine at Peştişu Mare.
Gold mine at Petroşani. Simion says 'gold ore was washed here (a bust of Ares was discovered in one of the washing installations).'

Archaeological site of Ruda-Brad. Two mine galleries; Ruda 12 Apostoli and Zdrahonţ-Saint John; also “Treptele Romane” (“The Roman Steps”).

Archaeological site of Săcărâmb - gold mine. Simion says: 'The Romans exploited only the gold tellurium (later called “săcărâmb”, silvanite) and only where it was visible to the naked eye. The ore left by the Romans inside the galleries contained gold up to 30 g/ton. At an altitude of aproximately 780 m, at the southern end of the Cetraş massif, there were ancient exploitations (Roman?) with a N-S orientation that M. J. Ackner explored along 25 m in length.'
Archaeological site of Săcărâmb - copper mine.

Mining - Gallery 1 at Sălişte-Dealul Draica. 'In the eastern part of the Băiţa mining basin there is a gold-silver exploitation at Draica; gold has been mined here since the Late Bronze Age, but also in the medieval period.' (RAN entry). Traces of a collapsed gallery.

Mining - Gallery 2 at Sălişte-Dealul Draica. 'In the eastern part of the Băiţa mining basin there is a gold-silver exploitation at Draica; gold has been mined here since the Late Bronze Age, but also in the medieval period.' (RAN entry). Traces of a collapsed gallery.
Brass mines' ('Minele de aramă') at Sândominic - Bălan - so zinc, and perhaps copper too?
Roman mine at Sasca Montană - Dealul Tecla.
Archaeological site of Sasca Romană - Sasca Romană  mine opened in Banatul Timişoarei, on the Besedin Hill.

Simion: 'Along the Arieş river are indicated traces of possible installation for gold washing from

Archaeological site of Slatina-Timiş - Mina Slatina gold mine.
Archaeological site of Stănija - Mina Stănija. Copper mine.

Roman iron mine at Ştinăpari - Dealul Chelu.
Roman mine at Surducu Mare - Mina Surducu Mare. Gold, silver, copper, and lead.

Archaeological site of Teliucu Inferior - Ploţca. 'The exploitation of iron dates from the period before Roman rule, but also from this time. Daco-Roman period iron processing workshop at Ticvaniu Mic - Sălişte.
Roman gold mine at Topliţa - Măgura Topliţa.

Gold mine at Trestia-Dealul Mialu - Roman gallery 1. 'There are traces of collapsed galleries in the area of ​​Sibilla, Maria Victoria, Istvan mines; In such a gallery, according to Téglás G., the skeletons of some miners (?) in chains, attributed to the non-free workers from the mines of Roman Dacia, would have been discovered.' Archaeological site of Vetel. Copper mine.
Traces of underground mining, and habitations of the Roman period, on the SE and NW slopes of Dumbrava hill.

Traces of Roman gold-washing installations along the river, mentioned in the 19th c.; chance finds of coins of the 2nd and 3rd c. AD (Simion, Téglàs)

In the late nineteenth century archaeological remains of the Roman period (gold mine, miners' housing) were discovered. Exploitation continued into the medieval period.

Alluvial hydraulic gold mining site; there were three large zanja-channels in the NE part of the zone, uniting to form a large zanja in the central part, with the stone dumps towards the Arroyo de Velasco in the SW. Now destroyed by modern quarrying.
Hydraulic mining with channels, reusing ditch of Castro de Rivas
Hydraulic mining with channels, reusing ditches of castro of La Salina.
Hydraulic mining; four fan-shaped channels, roughly S-N, uniting to form a long single channel discharging into the Arroyo de Paradilla

The Catálogo de bienes protegidos for Castilla y Leon says that the ditches of the Corona were made with hydraulic power [this is clearly wrong, and there are "murias" (clearance piles of stones) from Roman mining operations.
Underground mine with a chamber covering about 30 m2 and three galleries leading off it. Waste dumps outside. Discovered in 2022.

Underground mine with several connected galleries, some up to 2 m in height. Discovered in 2023 (reported 14 August 2023). Alluvial mine in old river terrace so earth from the underground mine had to be taken out to be washed outside the mine.

A series of small scale workings along the slope of the ridge to the W of the motorway intersection by Pradorrey. A channel comes from the W, and at least six small-scale ditches divert from it down the slope to the south. These look either like prospections, or were very small-scale mining operations. Probably the channel continued eastward to feed the mine at Pradorrey, but the intervening stretch has been destroyed by the motorway intersection.

Small hydraulic mine working; a channel coming from the S bifurcates around an oval area in the centre of the working (resembling a corona, but the ditches are too shallow), and converge again in two exit ditches towards the stream. The eastern side is also fed by another ditch from the SE.

Large hydraulic opencast associated with (and partly destroying) the castro of Los Castros - La Forcada. Apparently ground sluicing in the northern part and deeper workings, with hushing, to the south.
